title: The past tense: strong verbs
title_target: Ég kom, ég sá, ég fór
goal: Master the verb group that adds no ending at all but changes the vowel inside the word — and that happens to contain the words you say most often.
bekal: form the past tense of *koma*, *fara*, *taka*, *sjá*, *fá*, and ten other strong verbs
tell a whole event from beginning to end

notes: **Strong verbs add nothing — they change the vowel inside the word.** *Koma → kom*, *fara → fór*, *taka → tók*, *sjá → sá*, *fá → fékk*. The *ég* form has **no ending at all**, and that's the easiest way to spot them. English does the same: *come → came*, *take → took*, *see → saw*.
**The *þú* form adds -st**, not *-r*: *þú komst*, *þú fórst*, *þú tókst*, *þú sást*. This is the only place in all of Icelandic where the ending *-st* marks the second person.
**About 150 Icelandic verbs are strong** — a small number compared with the thousands of weak ones. But they include almost every word you use daily, so the load feels bigger than the number.
**Fékk mér pylsu — fá sér means "get something for yourself".** It's used for eating and drinking: *fá sér kaffi*, *fá sér bjór*, *fá sér að borða*. The closest English is "grab" or "have".

**Var þegar komin upp — a form you haven't learned yet.** *Komin* is the *sagnbót* (supine), part of the "have done" construction: that's unit 17. For now, just notice that forms ending in *-inn/-in/-ið* often mark a finished action.

**Apollo astronauts really did train in Iceland.** In 1965 and 1967, Apollo crew candidates — including Neil Armstrong — were sent to the Askja lava plains to learn to recognize volcanic rock. NASA chose Iceland because its surface was considered the most moon-like on Earth.

grammars.title: The six forms of strong verbs
body: Notice three things: the *ég* form has no ending, the *þú* form has *-st*, and the plural often changes vowel again.
after: *Vera* is the most important verb and also the most irregular: **var, varst, var, vorum, voruð, voru**. Learn these six forms before any others — they show up in almost every sentence about the past.
The plural almost always keeps the singular vowel, except for *vera* (*var → vorum*) and a few others. If in doubt, keep the singular vowel; you'll be right nine times out of ten.

grammars.title: The twenty most common strong verbs
body: This list is worth pinning on your wall. The middle column is the past *ég* form — that's the one that needs to stick.
after: ⚠️ *Halda* has two equally common meanings: "hold" and "think (believe)". *Ég hélt að þú værir farinn* — I thought you'd left. The second is far more common in conversation.
*Eiga → átti* is actually half weak, half strong, like *segja → sagði* and *þykja → þótti*. This mixed group is small, but all its members are common.

blocks.text: A story isn't just a string of past-tense sentences; it needs linking words to set the order. Here are the most common ones, and what they do to word order.

blocks.title: The verb-second rule strikes again
items: If your sentence opens with *svo*, *þá*, *síðan*, or any time expression, **the verb jumps ahead of the subject**: *Svo **fór ég** heim*, not *svo ég fór heim*.
But after *og*, *en*, and *af því að*, the order stays normal: *… **og ég fór** heim*. You need to tell these two groups apart, and your ear will pick it up faster than the rule.

blocks.text: These eight sentences are the skeleton of any story. Swap in your own things and times, and you can already tell the story of your own first experience — the most useful speaking practice at this level.
